item.title: Global Market Today: Asian shares cautious as AI selloff fears persist despite US futures rebound
item.description: US Treasury futures declined in early Asian trading as demand for haven assets ebbed. Brent crude fell 0.8% to around $91.80 a barrel, while spot gold rallied 1.1% to about $3,575 an ounce after five straight days of losses. Cash trading in US Treasuries is closed during Asian hours due to Japan’s holiday.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: US equity-index futures opened higher in early Asian trading as buyers returned following Friday’s sharp selloff sparked by an unwinding of the artificial intelligence trade. Treasury bond futures fell.Contracts for the S&P 500 Index rose 1.9% and those for the Nasdaq 100 Index climbed 2.6%.Still, a tone of caution persisted in Asia, with Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc. — among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI trade — opening lower. The Kospi Index in South Korea fell 2.6% in early trading. Equities in Australia edged down, while Japanese markets are closed Monday for a holiday.Read more: Stocks in news: Adani Energy, Maruti Suzuki, RailTel, Waaree Energies and Indian Bank“We reiterate our view that the recent pullback in risk assets is mostly an AI de-leveraging event amidst weak sentiment, coupled with a more hawkish Fed reaction function being priced in,” JPMorgan analysts said in a note. “We keep the faith in the durability of the AI supercycle, supported by lower leverage and improved positioning.”Elsewhere in markets, US Treasury futures declined in early Asian trading as demand for haven assets ebbed. Brent crude fell 0.8% to around $91.80 a barrel, while spot gold rallied 1.1% to about $3,575 an ounce after five straight days of losses. Cash trading in US Treasuries is closed during Asian hours due to Japan’s holiday.Traders in Asia were bracing for another bout of volatility even as regional authorities stepped up efforts to shore up markets. On Friday, the S&P 500 entered a technical correction and the Nasdaq 100 posted its worst week since March 2020. The VIX Index, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, surged to its highest since April 2025.Goldman Sachs Group Inc.’s trading desk says last week’s selloff has created an attractive opportunity to snap up US stocks. Still, the bank cautioned that overall investor positioning remains elevated, signaling the broader capitulation needed for a meaningful rally could be missing.“Generally speaking, panic like we’ve recently seen has been a good opportunity to start adding risk,” the bank’s traders wrote in the note.Friday’s retreat fueled concern that the US technology selloff is broadening into a wider risk-off move. MSCI’s gauge for Asia Pacific equities is near a bear market after falling about 18% from its June peak, putting the focus on whether authorities can help restore confidence and stem further selling.Officials across Asia stepped up efforts over the weekend to stem the deepening stock-market rout. China will ease minimum margin requirements for investors buying securities with borrowed funds, while Taiwan widened curbs on short selling and said it has been buying shares after the island’s benchmark suffered its worst weekly drop in 35 years.South Korean authorities said they will ease daily limits on company share buybacks for three months and begin preparations to activate a stock-market stabilization fund if needed. The rescue fund was last used during the global financial crisis in 2008, according to local media.Investors are also looking ahead to US inflation data this week. Economists expect the personal consumption expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, to have risen 3.8% in October from a year earlier, according to the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey. The figures are due Wednesday in a Thanksgiving holiday-shortened week.Still, Friday’s market rout, driven by an unwinding of bets on AI-led growth, prompted traders to pare expectations for a December interest-rate hike as investors piled into Treasuries.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Sunday that the Fed risks damaging the US economy by overtightening in response to the latest inflation data, pointing to signs of fragility in the financial system.“Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they overtighten,” Bessent told CBS’s Face The Nation, noting a series of hawkish comments from the central bank’s governors in recent weeks. “We’ve seen a substantial tightening in financial conditions over the past few months.”

item.title: Sensex surges 20% in dollar terms as foreign money chases India
item.description: The Sensex has increased by 20% in dollar terms this quarter, marking a potential bull market. Foreign fund flows have contributed significantly to this surge, driven by global investors seeking diversification. The rupee's appreciation has also enhanced returns for foreign investors holding Indian assets. Despite recent gains, many investors remain cautious and have yet to fully engage in the Indian market.
item.dc:creator: Ravindra Sonavane
item.content:encoded: Mumbai: The Sensex has surged 20% in dollar terms this quarter, charging into what the Street describes as a bull-market zone, as record foreign fund flows in the fortnights either side of Diwali have made a sparkling rupee the envy of a dispirited Asia-Pacific in the throes of the AI meltdown. Around 15-16% of the gains in dollar terms came from rising share prices, while 4-5% was contributed by the rupee's appreciation, said Manishi Raychaudhuri, CEO of Hong Kong-based Emmer Capital Partners.Emerging market investors, who were significantly underweight on India, have been prominent buyers as funds move away from crowded AI trades toward the Indian markets, said Raychaudhuri.136086057The Sensex has logged the steepest gains since the Covid year after shrinking nearly a fifth in dollar terms through the first three quarters of 2026. The Nifty 50 has gained 18.2%, with both indices lately heading equity leader-boards globally.An index jump of 20% or more is widely regarded as the threshold for a bull market. This is more of a market convention rather than a formal rule.In rupee terms, both indices have risen around 16% each. The rupee has appreciated 3.4% against the dollar so far this quarter, boosting foreign investors' returns when their Indian investments are converted into the US currency.The last time the indices recorded sharper gains was in the December 2020 quarter, when both gauges rose nearly 26% in dollar terms.Read more: India does not have FANGs or MANGOes, but has WITCH companies, says PPFAS Mutual Fund’s Rajeev ThakkarSince October 16, when foreigners started buying stocks here again, overseas investors have pumped $14.33 billion, or approximately ₹1.43 lakh crore, into the market here. Of the 24 trading sessions since then, they have been buyers in 20. We've already seen some buying, but I think we're still at the 'beginning of the beginning', with scope for those inflows to continue over the coming months, said Ben Powell, chief investment strategist for the Middle East and Asia-Pacific, BlackRock Investment Institute.Powell said India's expanding workforce, rising productivity and digitalisation offered global investors diversification benefits at a time when many markets were becoming an AI trade in disguise. Foreign investors had sold nearly $55 billion worth of Indian equities between October 2024 and September 2026. So far in the December quarter, FPIs invested $10.4 billion in India, the second-highest inflow after Japan's $48 billion.South Korea and Taiwan, investor favourites through early 2026, saw outflows of $26 billion and $57 billion, respectively, according to Bloomberg data.Read more: Nifty scales nine-month high, 26K in sight: 5 triggers that could drive or derail D-Street rally this weekThe rally comes as global markets have corrected amid concerns over AI and technology stocks, higher interest rates, inflation and policy uncertainty. During the same period, the S&P 500 fell 10%, while the Dow Jones and Nasdaq declined 5% and 16%, respectively. China's Shenzhen and Hang Seng indices lost 9% each, while Japan's Nikkei fell 16% in dollar terms. Taiwan's Taiex and South Korea's Kospi declined around 28%, Indonesia's Jakarta Composite fell 17%, and the Philippines lost 8%.The UK's FTSE 100 and Germany's DAX slipped 4% each, while France's CAC 40 declined 0.5%.Raychaudhuri said many investors were yet to return to the Indian market. There's still a significant population of investors who are on the sidelines of the India trade or who have just nibbled it a bit. The underweight positions on India were so large that it's difficult for it to have come to a neutral tilt in just about three weeks or so, he said.
